title: Suspending the Gas Tax Won’t Help
author: Peter Hart
content:
[![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/05/IMG_1912-2-680x475.jpeg)](https://www.counterpunch.org/2026/05/22/suspending-
the-gas-tax-wont-help/)

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/05/IMG_1912-2-680x475.jpeg)

Shell station, West Linn, Oregon. (This was the price on May 2. It's 10 cents
higher now.)

In response to a question about the Iran War, President Trump (famously)
[said](https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/donald-trump/trump-not-thinking-
american-finances-iran-talk-rcna344785) “I don’t think about Americans’
financial situation.” Around the same time, though, the White House was
floating a policy that seemed designed to offer relief from rising gas prices:
Suspending the federal gas tax. The policy is emblematic of the Trump brand of
populism – something that sounds good but would do very little.

Before considering its political viability, it’s worth understanding why this
is not a very good idea in the first place. The current federal gasoline tax –
18.4 cents per gallon – supports the underfunded Highway Trust Fund, which is
estimated to be [depleted in the next few
years](https://www.everycrsreport.com/reports/R48948.html). The Highway Trust
Fund allocates money toward highway and mass transit projects by providing
grants to state and local governments. Given the massive infrastructure
problems facing the country – which the public overwhelmingly wants the
government to spend money to fix – a policy that delivers even less money for
repairs to our roads, subways, and bridges would be unwise. (The current
federal tax [has not increased since 1993](https://itep.org/an-unhappy-
anniversary-federal-gas-tax-reaches-25-years-of-stagnation/); if anything, one
could make a strong argument that the gas tax is too low).

Would suspending it save money? Not much. Estimates
[vary](https://bipartisanpolicy.org/explainer/the-hidden-cost-of-a-gas-tax-
holiday/); the [Penn Wharton Budget
Mode](https://budgetmodel.wharton.upenn.edu/blog/BE2026-3/)l suggests that
consumers might get “60 to 72 percent of the tax savings at the pump, with the
remainder captured by suppliers.”

Ironically, the last president to suggest a gas tax holiday was President Joe
Biden, who floated the idea in 2022 in response to the spiking prices linked
to the Russian invasion of Ukraine. Some Republicans who [opposed the idea
when it came from Biden](https://www.thebulwark.com/p/republicans-gas-tax-
holiday-trump-biden) are now somewhat supportive of Trump’s plan.

Does that mean it’s more likely to happen this time around? There are already
gas tax bills in the [House](https://www.congress.gov/bill/119th-
congress/house-bill/7919/text?s=3&r=8) and
[Senate,](https://www.congress.gov/bill/119th-congress/senate-bill/4032/text)
so it remains to be seen if there is any real momentum to enact such a policy.
But if the goal is to deliver relief to the public, there are other options
available. For instance, CEPR senior economist Dean Baker
[suggested](https://cepr.net/publications/the-perfect-gift-for-trumps-friends-
in-the-oil-industry-a-windfall-profits-tax/) a windfall profits tax: “We can
simply tax back some of the money we’re handing over to the industry because
of the Iran war and send it to people in the form of rebate checks, similar to
the $2,000 pandemic checks we got in 2021.”

The chances of passing Trump’s preferred policy might be slim, and the odds of
Trump supporting a tax on the oil companies that [helped power his
victory](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2025/jan/23/big-oil-445m-trump-
congress) might be zero. But other policymakers could take up the cause.
